what_it_does: Training a large language model requires enormous amounts of GPU memory because the system must remember every intermediate calculation (called activations — the values produced at each layer as data flows forward through the network) so it can compute gradients on the backward pass. As models grow larger, these activations can dwarf the GPU's memory capacity, forcing smaller batches and slower training. SSDTrain proposes offloading those intermediate values to high-capacity consumer solid-state drives (NVMe SSDs) instead of keeping them in expensive GPU memory. The key engineering challenge is that SSDs are much slower than GPU memory, so the system carefully overlaps data transfers with ongoing computation so neither the GPU nor the SSD sits idle waiting for the other. It also deduplicates repeated tensor values before sending them to the SSD, reducing how much data needs to move. The approach is described as plugging into standard training frameworks (PyTorch, Megatron, DeepSpeed) without requiring model rewrites, though concrete speed numbers are not given in the abstract.
